lines.text: however, this truth is not expressed in its generality but
from a quite special angle; it is a question of the history of
the disciples of Jesus, of the first Christian community, of
the visible and apparent aspect of this history as contrasted
with its invisible fundamental truth and reality. The theme
is the forsakenness of this little flock in the world, and, in
conjunction with that, its superiority to the world. For in
truth the evangelist does not propose to depict a farewell
scene in a moving and poetical way, but in the situation of
the disciples he is symbolizing the situation of the Christian
fellowship as a whole. Their fate is ours; the promise made
to them is likewise made to us.
The picture given of the disciples being left by Jesus to
face, alone, a hostile world is not a picture of some transient
episode but of the situation of the Christian community in
the world at all times. Nor is it a scene which recurs only
occasionally in periods of special crisis and stress, but it
expresses the essential character of the universal Christian
situation: namely, its abandonment in the great world. Why
does this feature belong to the very essence of its life? The
context of the passage we have chosen as our text makes this
quite plain: believers in Him are the friends of Jesus whom
He has chosen out of the world (15: I4ff.) and who belong
to Him. This tie with Jesus means also however an indis-
soluble connexion with His fate. It is a link of a different
kind from that which binds disciples to a great teacher or
leader of humanity who brings to birth new insights and
new ideals and initiates new tasks and programmes. Of
course in this latter case too the disciples' association with
their leader can involve a sharing of his fate, a participation
not only in his ideals and aspirations, but also in his struggles,
sacrifices and sufferings. Yet this is only true in a partial
sense and usually only at the beginning of the movement
when it is necessary to struggle for an acceptance of the new
ideas in the world. Discipleship to Jesus, on the other hand,
means necessarily and always a real sharing of His fate.
This fate implies facing the mistrust and enmity of the
